title: The Brain-Freeze Smoothie
briefing: Tomás, 14, gulps a frozen smoothie through a straw on a hot day. A few seconds later a sharp ache hits his forehead. It fades in about half a minute — and when he goes back to slow sips, it doesn't happen again.
question: Why does something cold in his mouth make his forehead hurt?

clues.title: Forehead ache
clues.text: A few seconds after a big gulp, a sharp ache hits right behind his forehead. Nothing touched his forehead at all.
clues.shows: pain felt in the forehead right after something cold in the mouth

clues.title: Only big gulps
clues.text: Slow sips of the same smoothie never hurt. Big gulps that hit the roof of his mouth always do.
clues.shows: the ache depending on cold hitting the roof of the mouth fast

clues.title: Tongue to the roof
clues.text: When he presses his warm tongue against the roof of his mouth, the ache fades faster.
clues.shows: warming the roof of the mouth easing the pain

clues.title: Gone in 30 seconds
clues.text: The ache fades in about half a minute and leaves no trace. His friend gets exactly the same thing from ice cream.
clues.shows: a short, harmless signal that switches off by itself

hypotheses.text: The cold on the roof of his mouth made blood vessels there squeeze and then rush open; nerves near those vessels send pain signals that his brain feels as coming from his forehead.
The cold is freezing his brain.
hypotheses.flaw: His brain sits deep inside his skull and stays warm; and warming the roof of his mouth with his tongue — nowhere near his brain — made the ache fade faster.

hypotheses.text: He is allergic to the smoothie.
hypotheses.flaw: Slow sips of the same smoothie caused no ache at all — so it is the cold and the speed, not what's in it.

hypotheses.text: Drinking through a straw makes you dizzy.
hypotheses.flaw: Slow sips through the same straw were fine; the ache came only when big gulps of cold hit the roof of his mouth.

prediction.prompt: As Tomás drinks faster — from slow sips to huge gulps — what happens to the forehead ache?

second.question: And as the seconds pass after the gulp?

transfer.context: Chloe bites straight into an ice-pop on a hot day and feels a stab of pain between her eyes for a few seconds.
options: She cracked a tooth on the ice-pop.
Cold on the roof of her mouth made nearby blood vessels squeeze and then rush open, and nerves there send pain that her brain feels in her forehead.
Ice-pops freeze the brain for a moment.
transfer.retryHint: Cold, fast, and the pain felt somewhere else — which of Tomás's clues showed the cold had to hit the roof of the mouth?
transfer.explanation: Chloe's brain didn't freeze. The ice-pop chilled the roof of her mouth fast, the blood vessels there squeezed and then rushed open, and the nerves nearby sent a pain signal that her brain reads as coming from her forehead — the same short, harmless ache Tomás got.

takeaway: A brain freeze isn't your brain freezing. Cold on the roof of your mouth makes blood vessels squeeze and then rush open, and the nerves there send a signal your brain feels as a forehead ache — short, harmless and gone in seconds.
